result: Visual bursts in the superior colliculus (SC) can occur intra-saccadically. The authors demonstrate that visually induced action potentials in the SC occurred during ongoing saccadic eye movements, with mild but significant modulations of visual burst strength depending on microsaccade direction relative to the receptive field location.
evaluation: Claims C1, C31, C32, and C33 are directly supported by experimental data showing visual bursts during saccades (Figure 2C). Statistical analysis confirms mild but significant modulations (t(137)=2.842, p=0.005). The directional modulation (C34) is consistent with prior work and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

result: Movement-related bursts in rostral SC occur simultaneously with peripheral visual bursts in caudal SC during microsaccades. The authors demonstrate through simultaneous recordings that rostral SC neurons exhibit movement-related bursts when microsaccades are triggered during peripheral visual bursts, while rostral SC inhibition only occurs in the absence of microsaccades.
evaluation: Claims C3, C70-C75, and C109-C113 are strongly supported by experiment 3 data (Figures 8-12). Simultaneous recordings from rostral and caudal SC sites demonstrate concurrent bursts during microsaccades (Figure 10). Statistical analysis shows no significant alteration of rostral motor bursts by peripheral visual bursts (p=0.12539, N=42 neurons), while microsaccade amplitudes were significantly larger with peripheral visual bursts (p=7.9073×10⁻²⁷).

result: Microsaccades towards the receptive field are increased in size when they coincide with peripheral visual bursts, with the increase reflecting stimulus properties. The timing of microsaccadic effects shows a ~20 ms lag relative to SC visual bursts, consistent with efferent processing delays.
evaluation: Claims C29-C30 and C35-C39 are supported by behavioral data in Figures 2B and 3. Statistical analysis confirms contrast-dependent effects (F(2,713)=81.55, p<1.27427×10⁻³²) and temporal dynamics consistent with efferent delays. The relationship between visual burst properties and movement metrics is demonstrated across multiple stimulus conditions.

result: The number of intra-saccadic visual spikes per recorded neuron is linearly related to microsaccade amplitude increases for movements towards the receptive field. Each additional spike systematically increases movement amplitude, with no similar effect for movements opposite the receptive field.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43, C45-C47, and C83 are strongly supported by data in Figure 4. Statistical analysis demonstrates a significant linear relationship for towards movements (F=426, p<0.0001; slope=0.066294, t=20.644, p<0.0001) but not for opposite movements (F=2.22, p=0.137). The linear relationship is replicated across experiments 1 and 2.

result: Visual spiking activity in purely visual neurons is positively correlated with increased microsaccade amplitudes, though the effect is weaker than for visual-motor neurons. Individual injected spikes correlate remarkably well with saccade metric changes, with visual-motor neurons showing stronger effects than visual neurons.
evaluation: Claims C48, C115, and C116 are supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, showing positive correlations for both neuron types with differential effects. Claim C117 is supported by citations to prior research (Mohler and Wurtz, 1976) and is consistent with the observed differential effects.

result: The distance of extra spiking activity on the SC map from the planned movement vector matters, with diminishing returns for increasing eccentricity. However, the slope of the relationship between injected visual spikes and microsaccade amplitude always remained positive across all tested eccentricities.
evaluation: Claims C49-C52 and C96 are supported by statistical analysis showing a significant interaction between eccentricity and number of injected spikes (slope=-0.0080709, t=-14.585, p<0.0001). Figure 4—figure supplement 3 demonstrates weaker effects for eccentricities >4-5 deg, but the slope remains positive across all eccentricities, indicating consistent additive effects.

result: There is a tight time window around saccade onset (approximately -30 ms to +30 ms) in which movement-unrelated spikes can systematically modify ongoing eye movements. Visual bursts occurring pre- and intra-saccadically dramatically increase microsaccade amplitudes by two- to three-fold, with diminished effects after peak velocity.
evaluation: Claims C53-C58 and C69 are supported by detailed temporal analyses in Figures 5 and 6. The data show consistent timing of effects across amplitude bins, with the critical window being -30 to +30 ms from saccade onset. The diminished effect after peak velocity (C54) is consistent with efferent delays cited from prior research.

result: For movements opposite to the recorded neuron's receptive fields, there was a lower number of spikes during the peri-saccadic interval, suggesting it was easier to trigger microsaccades when no activity was present in the opposite SC.
evaluation: Claims C59 and C60 are supported by data in Figure 6B showing reduced spiking during the peri-saccadic interval for opposite movements. The inference that this facilitates movement triggering (C60) is reasonable given the data pattern, though it remains an interpretation.

result: Once a movement-unrelated spike is properly temporally aligned with the motor burst, it has similar behavioral impact on movement amplitudes regardless of eccentricity. The weaker global behavioral effects with more eccentric stimuli may reflect reduced likelihood of temporal alignment between visual spikes and the population of neurons bursting as part of the movement command.
evaluation: Claim C61 is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing similar quantitative effects with proper temporal alignment for both near and far neurons. Claim C62 is a reasonable inference based on the temporal alignment hypothesis from Jagadisan and Gandhi (2019) and the observed eccentricity effects, though it remains speculative.

result: Sustained discharge in SC neurons (outside of visual bursts) can also influence microsaccade amplitudes. For movements towards the receptive field, every additional sustained spike linearly increased microsaccade amplitude (slope=0.0126 deg/spike), though the impact per spike was smaller than during burst discharge.
evaluation: Claims C63-C68 are supported by data from experiment 2 (Figure 7). Statistical analysis confirms the linear relationship for sustained discharge (F=13.1, p=0.0364; slope=0.0126, t=3.61, p=0.0363). The smaller magnitude compared to burst discharge (C67) is expected given that fewer neurons are likely simultaneously active during sustained discharge.

result: The results suggest instantaneous readout of the SC during movement generation, irrespective of activity source, explaining a significant component of kinematic variability of motor outputs. The entire landscape of SC activity can instantaneously contribute to individual saccade metrics in a lawful manner, with detailed properties depending on the location of activity on the SC topographic map.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C17-C19, C76, C78, C80, and C82 represent the main conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experiments showing: (1) intra-saccadic visual bursts occur (Figures 2-3), (2) linear relationships between spike counts and movement metrics (Figures 4-7), (3) tight temporal windows for effects (Figures 5-6), and (4) eccentricity-dependent effects (Figure 4 supplements). The lawful, additive nature of the integration is demonstrated across multiple conditions.

result: The results are consistent with the mini-vector model in showing linear contributions of additional SC spikes, but add the notion that there need not be a classifier identifying movement-related versus irrelevant spikes. The model needs to consider local and remote interactions more explicitly, and the link between SC motor burst spiking and saccade kinematics is more loose than suggested by the model.
evaluation: Claims C94-C95, C97, C99, C102, and C104 represent critical evaluation of existing models. The consistency with linear contributions (C94) is supported by Figures 4, 6, and 7. The need for classifier-free readout (C95) and consideration of local/remote interactions (C97) are reasonable inferences from the eccentricity effects. The critique of the model's limitations (C99, C104) is supported by the data and citations to recent work (Peel et al., 2020).

result: The idea of temporal alignment from Jagadisan and Gandhi (2019) provides a plausible explanation for why the strongest impact of visual spikes on movement metrics was found in a specific time window around movement onset. The weaker behavioral effects with increasing eccentricity could be explained by more variable visual bursts of far neurons reducing the likelihood of temporal alignment.
evaluation: Claims C105-C108 integrate prior work (Jagadisan and Gandhi, 2019) with the current findings. The temporal alignment hypothesis (C105-C107) is well-supported by the tight temporal window observed in Figure 6. The explanation for eccentricity effects (C108) is speculative but reasonable given the cited differences in spatial frequency preferences (Chen et al., 2018) and the observed temporal patterns.

result: The additive mechanism might underlie effects in experimental psychophysics where saccade kinematics are altered by sudden irrelevant visual information. The results expose plausible neural mechanisms for behavioral effects on saccades accompanied by nearby visual flashes and motivate revisiting the role of the SC in saccade control from the perspective of visual-motor multiplexing.
evaluation: Claims C84-C93 and C118 represent speculative extensions and future directions. While the proposed mechanisms are plausible and consistent with the data, they remain hypotheses requiring additional testing. The connections to psychophysical effects (C84-C85), pursuit system (C86-C87), and blink studies (C88-C89) are supported by citations but not directly tested. Claims about future work (C90-C93) are reasonable suggestions but not empirical results.

result: Background claims about sensory-motor neurons, visual-motor neurons in various brain areas, SC models, and prior behavioral evidence. These establish the context and motivation for the current study.
evaluation: Claims C6-C16, C20-C21, C77, C79, C81, C98, C100-C101, and C103 are background claims supported by citations to prior research. These are appropriately cited and provide necessary context for the study. The accuracy of these claims depends on the cited literature, which appears to be appropriately referenced.

result: Methodological details about experimental design, subjects, and data collection. The experiments used appropriate methods including scleral search coil for eye tracking, multiple stimulus conditions, and careful control to ensure recorded neurons did not burst for microsaccade generation.
evaluation: Claims C22-C26 and C119-C124 describe experimental methods and are supported by the Materials and methods section and supplementary data. The verification that recording sites did not simultaneously burst for microsaccade generation (C24) is critical and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1. Sample sizes are clearly reported (84 neurons in experiment 1, 55 in experiment 2, 42 rostral and 54 caudal neurons in experiment 3).
